text.p: A source close to talks between German steel groups Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp and rival Thyssen AG to call off Krupp's hostile takeover bid in favour of a mutual venture have been progressing well, a source close to the talks said on Saturday.
"The talks are taking place in a good climate," the source told Reuters, noting the chances appeared good the two sides could reach a "letter of intent" by Thursday's deadline.

The talks, which began on Thursday at a secret location, so far have discussed that Thyssen, the larger of the two, would take over leadership of any venture between the two steel units -- Thyssen Steel AG and Krupp Hoesch Steel AG.
A top German union official who sits on the supervisory board of Krupp said earlier on Saturday she believed a takeover fight with rival Thyssen AG could end in mutual co-operation.

But tensions kept heating up as Thyssen's works council called on some 50,000 workers to stage a protest on Tuesday in Frankfurt, the nation's financial capital, and top politicans called on both companies to show social responsibility.

"We are going to Frankfurt because we fear that our future cannot be helped by the democratically-elected government in Bonn but will instead be decided by the banks," said Thyssen works council leader Georg Bongen in announcing the rally.
Karin Benz-Overhage, a top official of German union IG Metall, did not comment on the outcome Krupp supervisory board meeting on Saturday in Essen called to discuss strategy.
But she said, "We assume a mutual solution can be found."
The meeting took place as Germany's Die Welt newspaper reported on Saturday that Krupp plans to relaunch its hostile takeover bid for Thyssen as soon as the first week of April.

Citing reliable sources, the newspaper said Krupp believed Thyssen had only agreed to talks this week about a merger of their steel companies in order to win time to defend itself against a complete takeover.
Krupp has secured bank financing of 15 billion marks in the event that it has to acquire 100 percent of Thyssen's capital.
Krupp launched a rare hostile takeover of larger Thyssen earlier last week, offering shareholders 435 marks a share, a 25 percent premium over the previous day's share price.

A merger between Krupp and Thyssen would create one of the world's largest steel operations, but Krupp has said the full merger of the two companies would create cost savings in other areas as well, such as engineering and automotive components.

The takeover attempt sparked spontaneous work stoppages by thousands of steel workers in the Ruhr valley heartland and local politicians intervened, persuading the two companies to begin talks over a merger of just their steel companies.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, facing slumping approval due to record unemployment, and political rival Gerhard Schroeder of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Saturday both called on the rivals to find an amicable solution.

But Germany's Der Spiegel magazine said on Saturday that studies by Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank AG and investment bank Goldman Sachs showed a merger could show positive results for Krupp as early as in the spring of 1998.
The study assumed both companies could sell off a number of subsidiaries and that Krupp could repay debts from the takeover by the end of the year 2000.
A Krupp official denied the report.

Also on Saturday, Germany's Focus magazine said a top Deutsche Bank AG official did not rule out resigning from the Thyssen supervisory board after trade unions sharply criticised Deutsche and Dresdner Bank for their role in the takeover.

"I will not rule out that I will give up my mandate at the end of the meeting (on Thursday)," Ulrich Cartellieri, who represents Deutsche's shareholder interests on the Thyssen board, told the magazine in an interview.
